items.stem:
DOCUMENT-BASED QUESTION — TENNESSEE CONNECTION

Directions: Analyze the following three primary sources. Apply the HIPP framework (Historical context, Intended audience, Purpose, Point of view) to each document. Then construct a multi-paragraph argument responding to the central question: How did the Nashville sit-in movement of 1960 advance a distinctive model of nonviolent direct action that transformed the Civil Rights Movement nationally?

---
Document 1: Paraphrase of James Lawson's nonviolent-resistance teaching as delivered in his 1959–1960 Nashville workshops at Clark Memorial Methodist Church and First Baptist Church. Sources: Rev. James Lawson, oral-history interview, *Eyes on the Prize* / Civil Rights Movement Veterans archive, https://www.crmvet.org/nars/lawsonj.htm; Bobby L. Lovett, *The Civil Rights Movement in Tennessee* (Univ. of Tennessee Press, 2005); summarized for instructional use — students should treat as a synthesis of Lawson's workshop philosophy rather than a verbatim address.

"We are not seeking to humiliate the white community. We are seeking to awaken their conscience and our own. Nonviolence is not passive — it is the most demanding form of courage. To sit at that counter and absorb hatred without responding with hatred, to maintain your dignity while every force around you denies it — that is an act of power, not weakness. We must be willing to fill the jails. The whole system of segregation depends on our cooperation with it. When we withdraw that cooperation, the system has no power."

---
Document 2: Excerpt from a statement by Diane Nash, Nashville sit-in leader, following her confrontation with Mayor Ben West on the courthouse steps, April 19, 1960. Source: Diane Nash, public statement, April 19–20, 1960; reported in The Nashville Tennessean, April 20, 1960; collected in Nashville Public Library Civil Rights Collection, Tennessee State Library and Archives, tn.gov/tsla.

"I asked the mayor directly: 'Mayor West, do you feel it is wrong to discriminate against a person solely on the basis of their race or color?' He said yes. Once he said yes, I knew the battle was won. He had to follow his own conscience — and he did. On May 10th, the lunch counters were desegregated. This is what nonviolent direct action can accomplish. It does not just change policy. It changes people."

---
Document 3: Excerpt from the founding statement of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee (SNCC), adopted at Shaw University, Raleigh, North Carolina, April 1960, drafted with the participation of Nashville student delegates including Diane Nash and John Lewis. Source: SNCC Statement of Purpose, April 1960; archived at the Library of Congress, Civil Rights Collections, loc.gov.

"We affirm the philosophical or religious ideal of nonviolence as the foundation of our purpose, the presupposition of our faith, and the manner of our action. Nonviolence as it grows from Judaic-Christian tradition seeks a social order of justice permeated by love. Integration of human endeavor represents the first step towards such a society... Through nonviolence, courage displaces fear; love transforms hate. Acceptance dissipates prejudice; hope ends despair. Peace dominates war; faith reconciles doubt."

---
Using all three documents and your knowledge of the Civil Rights Movement, construct a multi-paragraph argument that (1) identifies the specific philosophical contributions Lawson (Document 1) made to the Nashville students' understanding of nonviolent direct action, (2) analyzes how Nash's courthouse confrontation (Document 2) represented a distinct application of the 'withdraw cooperation' strategy to a moment of moral accountability, (3) explains how the Nashville students' ideas — captured in Document 3 — shaped the national civil rights infrastructure through SNCC, and (4) evaluates whether the Nashville model represented a more disciplined or more radical vision of nonviolent direct action compared to the Montgomery Bus Boycott approach (US.72).
items.stemEs:
PREGUNTA BASADA EN DOCUMENTOS — CONEXIÓN CON TENNESSEE

Instrucciones: Analice las siguientes tres fuentes primarias. Aplique el marco HIPP (Contexto histórico, Audiencia prevista, Propósito, Punto de vista) a cada documento. Luego construya un argumento de varios párrafos en respuesta a la pregunta central: ¿Cómo el movimiento de sentadas de Nashville de 1960 avanzó un modelo distintivo de acción directa no violenta que transformó el Movimiento de Derechos Civiles a nivel nacional?

---
Documento 1: Extracto del discurso de James Lawson ante la Conferencia Nacional sobre Resistencia No Violenta, Nashville, Tennessee, 1960. Fuente: James Lawson, discurso ante los organizadores de las sentadas de Nashville, 1960; Colección de Derechos Civiles de la Biblioteca Pública de Nashville, Colecciones Especiales; colecciones digitales de la Biblioteca y Archivos Estatales de Tennessee, tn.gov/tsla.

"No buscamos humillar a la comunidad blanca. Buscamos despertar su conciencia y la nuestra. La no violencia no es pasiva — es la forma más exigente de coraje. Sentarse en ese mostrador y absorber el odio sin responder con odio, mantener tu dignidad mientras cada fuerza a tu alrededor la niega — ese es un acto de poder, no de debilidad. Debemos estar dispuestos a llenar las cárceles. Todo el sistema de segregación depende de nuestra cooperación con él. Cuando retiramos esa cooperación, el sistema no tiene poder."

---
Documento 2: Extracto de una declaración de Diane Nash, líder de las sentadas de Nashville, tras su confrontación con el alcalde Ben West en los escalones del juzgado, 19 de abril de 1960. Fuente: Diane Nash, declaración pública, 19–20 de abril de 1960; reportado en The Nashville Tennessean, 20 de abril de 1960; recogido en la Colección de Derechos Civiles de la Biblioteca Pública de Nashville, Archivos y Biblioteca Estatal de Tennessee, tn.gov/tsla.

"Le pregunté directamente al alcalde: '¿Alcalde West, cree usted que es malo discriminar a una persona únicamente en base a su raza o color?' Dijo que sí. Una vez que dijo que sí, supe que la batalla estaba ganada. Tenía que seguir su propia conciencia — y lo hizo. El 10 de mayo, los mostradores del almuerzo fueron desegregados. Esto es lo que puede lograr la acción directa no violenta. No solo cambia las políticas. Cambia a las personas."

---
Documento 3: Extracto de la declaración fundacional del Comité Estudiantil No Violento de Coordinación (SNCC), adoptada en la Universidad Shaw, Raleigh, Carolina del Norte, abril de 1960, redactada con la participación de delegados estudiantiles de Nashville, incluyendo a Diane Nash y John Lewis. Fuente: Declaración de Propósito del SNCC, abril de 1960; archivada en la Biblioteca del Congreso, Colecciones de Derechos Civiles, loc.gov.

"Afirmamos el ideal filosófico o religioso de la no violencia como el fundamento de nuestro propósito, el presupuesto de nuestra fe y la manera de nuestra acción. La no violencia tal como surge de la tradición judeo-cristiana busca un orden social de justicia impregnado de amor. La integración del esfuerzo humano representa el primer paso hacia tal sociedad... A través de la no violencia, el coraje desplaza al miedo; el amor transforma el odio. La aceptación disipa el prejuicio; la esperanza termina con la desesperación. La paz domina la guerra; la fe reconcilia la duda."

---
Usando los tres documentos y su conocimiento del Movimiento de Derechos Civiles, construya un argumento de varios párrafos que (1) identifique las contribuciones filosóficas específicas que Lawson (Documento 1) hizo a la comprensión de los estudiantes de Nashville sobre la acción directa no violenta, (2) analice cómo la confrontación de Nash en el juzgado (Documento 2) representó una aplicación distinta de la estrategia de 'retirar la cooperación' a un momento de responsabilidad moral, (3) explique cómo las ideas de los estudiantes de Nashville — capturadas en el Documento 3 — dieron forma a la infraestructura nacional de derechos civiles a través del SNCC, y (4) evalúe si el modelo de Nashville representó una visión más disciplinada o más radical de la acción directa no violenta en comparación con el enfoque del Boicot de Autobuses de Montgomery (US.72).
items.correctAnswer: A top-scoring (6/6) response would include: ARGUMENT THESIS: The Nashville sit-in movement, developed through Lawson's systematic training workshops and executed with unprecedented discipline, produced not just local desegregation but a nationally transferable model of nonviolent direct action — and the student leaders who emerged from Nashville (Nash, Lewis, Bevel) became the organizational backbone of SNCC and subsequent national campaigns. DOCUMENT 1 HIPP: Historical context: Early 1960, two years after Lawson had begun training Nashville students in Gandhian nonviolence following his study in India; in the immediate context of the Greensboro sit-ins (February 1, 1960) which spread to Nashville. Intended audience: Nashville student activists — the core group who had been training since 1959. Purpose: To articulate the philosophical framework of nonviolent direct action as an active, demanding form of courage — not mere passivity. To prepare students psychologically and philosophically for what they would face at the lunch counters. Point of view: Lawson as theological and strategic mentor, drawing on Gandhi, Thoreau, and Christian nonviolence traditions; representing a more systematic and philosophically developed approach than ad hoc protest. DOCUMENT 2 HIPP: Historical context: April 19, 1960 — the day Z. Alexander Looby's home was bombed, triggering a silent march of ~2,500 students to City Hall. Intended audience: The Nashville public and the broader Civil Rights Movement; also addressed to Mayor Ben West directly. Purpose: To document and publicize the moral logic of the direct confrontation — forcing West to affirm publicly that segregation was morally wrong and then holding him to that statement. Point of view: Nash as a disciplined, strategically sophisticated 22-year-old organizer who understood that public moral accountability was as powerful as economic pressure. DOCUMENT 3 HIPP: Historical context: April 1960, Shaw University — Ella Baker convened Nashville students and others who had been leading sit-ins; SNCC founded as student-led, independent of SCLC. Intended audience: The national civil rights community and student activists across the South. Purpose: To establish the philosophical and organizational foundation of SNCC as distinct from older civil rights organizations — student-led, philosophically committed to nonviolence, seeking systemic change. Point of view: Nashville students (Nash, Lewis, Bevel, Lafayette) who had internalized Lawson's framework and were now codifying it for a national audience. SYNTHESIS vs. MBB: Nashville was more systematically philosophical (structured training workshops vs. MBB's reactive formation) and more focused on direct-action confrontation of moral hypocrisy (Nash-West confrontation) vs. MBB's primarily economic and legal strategy. Both were nonviolent; Nashville's model was more intentionally replicable.
items.dokRationale: Student must synthesize across multiple standards and sources, constructing an extended argument that connects US.74, US.72 through evidence-based reasoning requiring sustained analytical writing.
items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (6 points):
6 - Exemplary: Student applies HIPP accurately and insightfully to all three documents with all four elements historically grounded. Constructs a sophisticated thesis about Nashville's distinctive philosophical contribution to the national movement. Analyzes Documents 1, 2, and 3 as interconnected evidence for a unified argument about the Nashville model's development and national spread. Accurately identifies the specific philosophical contributions (withdraw cooperation, moral accountability, SNCC founding). Makes a substantive comparative evaluation of Nashville vs. MBB models. Uses outside knowledge (Greensboro sit-ins, Ella Baker, Highlander Folk School, Freedom Rides) to enrich the argument. Writing is analytical, specific, and advances a defensible thesis.
5 - Advanced: HIPP applied accurately to all three documents with most elements present. Thesis addresses Nashville's distinctive contribution. Documents are analyzed rather than summarized. Makes a comparison to MBB with some analytical depth. Some outside knowledge used.
4 - Proficient: HIPP applied to all three documents with reasonable accuracy. Argument addresses the central question with evidence from all three documents. Comparison to MBB is present but somewhat superficial. Limited outside knowledge.
3 - Adequate: HIPP applied to two of three documents with reasonable accuracy. Argument addresses the central question but may be underdeveloped or rely on one or two documents. Comparison to MBB may be absent or very brief.
2 - Developing: HIPP attempted for one or two documents with partial accuracy. Argument is present but does not fully address the central question. Documents are summarized rather than analyzed.
1 - Beginning: Basic document summaries without HIPP. Argument absent or too vague. No comparison to MBB.
0 - No response or completely off-topic.

DOCUMENT ANALYSIS EXPECTATIONS: Doc 1 — Lawson's India study; 'withdraw cooperation' philosophy; nonviolence as active courage; preparing for jail; systemic analysis of segregation. Doc 2 — Looby bombing context; silent march; Nash's direct moral question to West; public accountability strategy; May 10 desegregation. Doc 3 — Ella Baker's role; SNCC's independence from SCLC; Nashville delegates (Nash, Lewis); philosophical foundation statement; judeo-christian nonviolence framework.
KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: James Lawson's 1959 training workshops at First Baptist Church Nashville; Greensboro sit-ins (Feb 1, 1960) sparking Nashville action; Z. Alexander Looby bombing; 2,500-person silent march; Nash-West courthouse confrontation; downtown Nashville desegregation May 10, 1960; Ella Baker's convening of Shaw conference; SNCC as student-led independent organization; Nash and Lewis as SNCC founders; Nashville students' leadership of Freedom Rides (1961).
items.explanationEs:
GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (6 puntos):
6 - Ejemplar: El estudiante aplica HIPP de manera precisa y perspicaz a los tres documentos con los cuatro elementos fundamentados históricamente. Construye una tesis sofisticada sobre la contribución filosófica distintiva de Nashville al movimiento nacional. Analiza los Documentos 1, 2 y 3 como evidencia interconectada para un argumento unificado sobre el desarrollo y la difusión nacional del modelo de Nashville. Identifica con precisión las contribuciones filosóficas específicas (retirar la cooperación, responsabilidad moral, fundación del SNCC). Hace una evaluación comparativa sustantiva del modelo de Nashville frente al de MBB. Usa conocimiento externo (sentadas de Greensboro, Ella Baker, Escuela Highlander Folk, Viajes de la Libertad) para enriquecer el argumento. La escritura es analítica, específica y avanza una tesis defendible.
5 - Avanzado: HIPP aplicado con precisión a los tres documentos con la mayoría de los elementos presentes. La tesis aborda la contribución distintiva de Nashville. Los documentos se analizan en lugar de resumirse. Hace una comparación con MBB con cierta profundidad analítica. Se usa algo de conocimiento externo.
4 - Competente: HIPP aplicado a los tres documentos con razonable precisión. El argumento aborda la pregunta central con evidencia de los tres documentos. La comparación con MBB está presente pero algo superficial. Conocimiento externo limitado.
3 - Adecuado: HIPP aplicado a dos de los tres documentos con razonable precisión. El argumento aborda la pregunta central pero puede estar poco desarrollado o depender de uno o dos documentos. La comparación con MBB puede estar ausente o ser muy breve.
2 - En desarrollo: HIPP intentado para uno o dos documentos con precisión parcial. El argumento está presente pero no aborda completamente la pregunta central. Los documentos se resumen en lugar de analizarse.
1 - Inicial: Resúmenes básicos de los documentos sin HIPP. Argumento ausente o demasiado vago. Sin comparación con MBB.
0 - Sin respuesta o completamente fuera del tema.

EXPECTATIVAS DE ANÁLISIS DE DOCUMENTOS: Doc 1 — Estudio de Lawson en India; filosofía de 'retirar la cooperación'; la no violencia como coraje activo; preparación para la cárcel; análisis sistémico de la segregación. Doc 2 — Contexto del atentado contra Looby; marcha silenciosa; pregunta moral directa de Nash a West; estrategia de responsabilidad pública; desegregación del 10 de mayo. Doc 3 — Papel de Ella Baker; independencia del SNCC del SCLC; delegados de Nashville (Nash, Lewis); declaración de fundamento filosófico; marco de no violencia judeo-cristiana.
EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Talleres de entrenamiento de James Lawson en 1959 en la Primera Iglesia Bautista de Nashville; sentadas de Greensboro (1 de febrero de 1960) que desencadenaron la acción en Nashville; atentado contra Z. Alexander Looby; marcha silenciosa de 2,500 personas; confrontación de Nash-West en el juzgado; desegregación del centro de Nashville el 10 de mayo de 1960; convocatoria de Ella Baker de la conferencia de Shaw; SNCC como organización independiente dirigida por estudiantes; Nash y Lewis como fundadores del SNCC; liderazgo de los estudiantes de Nashville en los Viajes de la Libertad (1961).
